title: Holistic health and care support for people experiencing homelessness in temporary accommodations (REACH)
official: Strengths-based, low caseload approach to integrated health, housing and practical support for people experiencing homelessness with multiple complex needs in temporary accommodations: a multi-centre, open-label, cluster randomised controlled trial with embedded economic and qualitative process evaluation
summary:
Background and study aims 
People who experience homelessness (PEH) suffer from poor physical and mental health. Many die in their early 40s as they do not receive timely help and treatment for their health and care needs. Most of these deaths can be prevented. Temporary accommodations (e.g. hostels) are often the first housing support for PEH. Despite housing some of the sickest citizens of society, there is no national guidance to tell us how health and care should be provided to temporary accommodation residents. Many residents with complex health and care issues struggle to move on as they are unable to receive the support they need. One person described to us that they spent 14 years in a hostel, mostly stuck in their room with mental health problems and no support. Many also return to the streets as they lack opportunities, and experience loneliness and boredom. 

This study will test a 'joined-up' way of delivering care in hostels. This has been called 'Reach, Engage and Recovery' (REACH) and it will involve mental health practitioners (e.g. mental health nurses) and care navigators providing support to temporary accommodation residents. 

Who can participate? 
Adults aged 18 or older who are a resident of a temporary accommodation, with one or more of the following: mental health problem, substance (includes alcohol) use, history of criminal justice encounter and/or equal to or longer than 6 months in one stay or repeat stay in temporary accommodations.

What does the study involve? 
The care team will have a low number of people to look after, which allows them to offer focused support for people who have high health and care needs. The care team will check, treat and refer people to improve their physical and mental health, wellbeing, practical skills for recovery and employment. This study will take place across  temporary accommodations for PEH based in London, Midlands, North of England and Scotland. Temporary accommodations will be divided into two groups, with residents of one group receiving the REACH care and the other group receiving the care as usual. 

The REACH group will receive support from the care team for 12 months, allowing rapport building over this period of contact and opportunities to establish positive changes. The REACH team will check residents' physical, mental health, housing, practical needs and provide trauma-informed (being aware of life situations) care. They will work with local community organisations to support skills (e.g. volunteering, gardening, mentoring, arts/crafts, employment training), address loneliness and promote wellbeing. They will focus on individual's strengths and goals as they support long-term recovery. Data will be collected to evaluate whether REACH reduces Emergency Department (A&E) visits, repeat homelessness, offending, resident deaths and improves housing uptake, quality of life and employment. Views will be obtained from PEH and service providers' views about REACH and the study will find out if it saves money for the health and care system. 

The study team have partnered with key national providers of hostels, health services and charities to better understand what is needed to roll out REACH across the UK. Study partners HomelessLink and Pathway will share the study findings with PEH, Government Departments and wider stakeholders. They plan to publish results in scientific journals and present the  findings in forms that are accessible to PEH. 

REACH was co-designed through discussions with members of a lived experience advisory group on homelessness at King's College London. They will remain advisors on the study. The study team also spoke to residents of temporary accommodations as well as frontline staff and managers. Participants recommended that REACH should focus on people who are most likely to fall through the gaps. One of the study's co-applicants has lived experience of homelessness.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
This study could help improve care for people who are experiencing homelessness. Participants in the intervention arm may receive additional support throughout the study. There are no anticipated risks or disadvantages of taking part in the study. Some questions may be upsetting but these are similar to questions in normal care.

Where is the study run from?  
King's College London, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
March 2027 to October 2029.

Who is funding the study? 
The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
Prf Vibhu Paudyal, vibhu.paudyal@kcl.ac.uk.
